'''Marvin Leonard''' "'''Murph'''" '''Goldberger''' (October 22, 1922 – November 26, 2014) was an American theoretical [[physicist]] who served as the [[University President|president]] of the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://history.aip.org/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?goldbergerm |title=Marvin "Murph" Goldberger, Array of Contemporary American Physicists |publisher=[[American Institute of Physics]] |access-date=July 5, 2018 |archive-date=April 20, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170420144312/http://history.aip.org/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?goldbergerm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name ="LATimes20141128" />

==Early life and education==
Goldberger was born in [[Chicago]], [[Illinois]]. He received his [[B.S.]] from the Carnegie Institute of Technology (now [[Carnegie Mellon University]]) and earned his [[Ph.D.]] in physics from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1948. His thesis advisor for ''Interaction of High-Energy Neutrons with Heavy Nuclei'' was Enrico Fermi.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/html/id.phtml?id=10736 |title=Marvin Leonard Goldberger |website=Mathematics Genealogy Project |access-date=January 10, 2007}}</ref><ref name="thesis-goldberger-1948">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/301816772/ |title=The interaction of high energy neutrons with heavy nuclei |date=1948 |publisher=[[The University of Chicago]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Goldberger |first=Marvin L.|id={{ProQuest|301816772}} |url-access=subscription  |oclc=44609154}}</ref> 

== Career ==
While serving in the Army shortly after graduation, he worked on the Manhattan Project under renowned physicist [[Enrico Fermi]] from 1943 to 1945.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-12-05 |title=Marvin L. Goldberger 1922–2014 - Press Release {{!}} Institute for Advanced Study |url=https://www.ias.edu/press-releases/marvin-l-goldberger-1922%E2%80%932014 |access-date=2023-10-13 |website=www.ias.edu |language=en}}</ref>

By at least 1951, Goldberger was a postdoc at MIT, where he shared a communal physics office  collaborated with [[Murray Gell-Mann]]. Goldberger suggested Gell-Mann join him at Chicago starting in 1952,<ref>Interview at https://www.webofstories.com/playAll/murray.gell-mann?sId=10555 (#35 of 200 few minute clips) accessed 28 Feb 2021</ref> before he became a professor of physics at [[Princeton University]] from 1957 to 1977. He received the [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics]] in 1961<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/heineman.cfm |title=Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics |website=[[American Physical Society]] |access-date=January 10, 2007}}</ref> and was elected to the [[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]] in 1963.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Marvin L. Goldberger |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/marvin-l-goldberger-zetiic/ |access-date=2022-06-21 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref> In 1965, he was elected a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Marvin L. Goldberger, past director |website=Institute for Advanced Study |date=December 9, 2019 |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/goldberger}}</ref> In 1980, he was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Marvin+Goldberger&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=2022-06-21 |website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> 

From 1978 to 1987, Goldberger served as the president of [[Caltech]]. He was the director of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] from 1987 to 1991.<ref>{{cite news |first=Anthony |last=DePalma |title=For Scholarly Nirvana, Familiar Questions as Leaders Change |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/06/26/education/for-scholarly-nirvana-familiar-questions-as-leaders-change.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm |quote=Dr. Goldberger, a former president of the California Institute of Technology, is a wry man who is able, despite his revered office (it belonged to J. Robert Oppenheimer from 1947 to 1966), to poke fun at himself. Given such an independent and strong-willed faculty, he said he sees the director's job as more that of pit crew than of car driver in this intellectual road race. |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 26, 1991 |access-date=January 14, 2011}}</ref> From 1991 to 1993, he was a professor of physics at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]]. From 1993 until his death in November 2014, he served on the faculty of the [[University of California, San Diego]], initially as a professor of physics and later as a professor emeritus. Goldberger also served as Dean of Natural Sciences for UC San Diego from 1994 to 1999.<ref name="LATimes20141128">{{cite news |first=Elaine |last=Woo |title=Marvin Goldberger dies at 92; physicist served as Caltech president
|url=http://www.latimes.com/local/obituaries/la-me-marvin-goldberger-20141129-story.html |quote=He left Caltech to become director of the Institute for Advanced Study, the Princeton, N.J., think tank that had been home to such luminaries as Einstein and J. Robert Oppenheimer. Goldberger held that post from 1987 to 1991, when he moved to UCLA to teach physics. He spent his last years at UC San Diego, where he was dean of the school of natural sciences from 1994 to 1999. |newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]] |date=November 28, 2014 |access-date=December 1, 2014}}</ref>

In 1954, he and [[Murray Gell-Mann]] introduced [[Crossing (physics)|crossing symmetry]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gell-Mann |first1=M. |last2=Goldberger |first2=M. L. |year=1954 |title=The scattering of low-energy photons by particles of spin ½. |journal=[[Physical Review]] |volume=96 |issue=5 |pages=1433–8 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.96.1433 |url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/60413/1/PhysRev.96.1433.pdf |bibcode=1954PhRv...96.1433G}}</ref> Four years later, he and [[Sam Treiman|Sam Bard Treiman]] published the so-called [[QCD vacuum#Goldberger–Treiman relation|Goldberger–Treiman relation]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Goldberger |first1=Marvin L. |last2=Treiman |first2=S.B. |title=Decay of the π Meson |journal=Physical Review |volume=110 |issue=5 |pages=1178 |year=1958 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.110.1178 |bibcode=1958PhRv..110.1178G|s2cid=50275209 |url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechAUTHORS:GOLpr58a |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Goldberger participated in [[Project 137]] in 1958 and became the first chairman of [[JASON (advisory group)|JASON]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2014-11-27 |title=Marvin L. "Murph" Goldberger |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/marvin-l-murph-goldberger-44963 |access-date=2026-09-02 |website=California Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Finkbeiner |first=Ann |date=2014-12-12 |title=Marvin Goldberger, Always Called "Murph": Part I |url=https://lastwordonnothing.com/2014/12/12/marvin-goldberger-always-called-murph-part-i/ |access-date=2026-09-02 |website=The Last Word On Nothing |language=en-US}}</ref> He was involved in nuclear arms control efforts. He also advised several major corporations; for example, he served on the board of directors of [[General Motors]] for 12 years.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/4630.html |title=Oral History Transcript — Dr. Marvin Goldberger |publisher=[[American Institute of Physics]] |date=February 12, 1986 |first=Finn |last=Aaserud |access-date=April 14, 2008 |archive-date=January 12, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150112060540/http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/4630.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Several of his doctoral students were elected Fellows of the American Physical Society: Allan N. Kaufman in 1962, Cyrus D. Cantrell in 1980, and Martin B. Einhorn in 1991.<ref>{{cite web |title=APS Fellowships |website=APS Physics |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/}}</ref> 

== Personal life ==
Goldberger died in November 2014 in [[La Jolla]], [[California]].<ref name=":0" /> His wife, [[Mildred Ginsberg Goldberger|Mildred Goldberger]], who also worked on the Manhattan Project, died in 2006.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/voices/oral-histories/mildred-goldbergers-interview/|title=Mildred Goldberger's Interview - Nuclear Museum}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Mildred (Ginsburg) Goldberger |website=Atomic Heritage Foundation |url=https://www.atomicheritage.org/profile/mildred-ginsberg-goldberger}}</ref> Upon his death he was survived by two sons and three grandchildren.<ref name="LATimes20141128" />
